title: Cook like a professional: stock, braise, grill and fry

say: Cook like a professional: stock, braise, grill and fry.
This is the video for Module 1 of Advanced Cooking and Nutrition: professional cooking techniques.
Professional cooks get the same result every time because they understand what heat, water, fat and time do to food.

say: Step one. Use bones with connective tissue, like chicken backs, necks and feet. Start them in cold water, covering the bones by about 5 cm.

Aromatics: about 10% of the bone weight
Simmer gently, never a hard boil
No salt; strain, label and chill

say: Step two. As it heats, skim off the grey foam.

say: Step three. Add aromatics, about one tenth of the bone weight: onion, garlic, ginger and thyme.

say: Step four. Keep it at a gentle simmer, with small bubbles just breaking the surface. The common mistake is a hard boil, which makes stock cloudy and greasy.

say: Bacteria grow fastest between about 5 C and 60 C. So divide hot stock into shallow containers, stand them in cold water, and refrigerate within 2 hours. Never leave stock on the stove overnight.

panel.rule: Cool stock in shallow containers; fridge within 2 hours.

say: Here is a worked example. Ifeoma covers 2 kg of chicken bones with 4 litres of cold water, skims, adds 200 g of aromatics, and simmers gently for 3 hours. She strains out about 3 litres.

card.title: A 3-litre chicken stock and its cost

say: Her bones cost about 5,000 naira, aromatics about 1,000 naira and gas about 800 naira.

card.title: A 3-litre chicken stock and its cost

say: That is about 6,800 naira, or about 2,267 naira per litre. She labels it, uses it within 3 days from the fridge, or freezes it in 500 ml bags.

say: Tough cuts are rich in collagen. Long, gentle, moist heat melts it into gelatin. First pat the meat dry, because wet meat steams instead of browning. Sear it in batches without crowding.

Judge by texture, not the clock
Plan backwards from serving time

say: Browning needs a dry surface and high heat, so pat food dry and leave space between pieces. Crowded pieces steam and turn grey.
The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food advise cooking food until it reaches 70 C. Probe the thickest part, away from the bone, then rest the meat.

say: Clear juices are helpful signs, but they are not proof.
Charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell that can kill. Never grill inside a room, kitchen or garage, even with a window open. And keep raw and cooked trays separate.

say: Oil that is too cool soaks into food. Oil that is too hot burns the outside first. Most frying works best at about 160 to 180 C.
Fry small batches, and fry yam, potato and plantain to golden, not dark brown.

cards.d: Most frying works at about 160 to 180 C. Fry small batches, golden not dark brown.
Oil no more than one third of the pot. Handle turned in. Never leave hot oil alone.
Never use water. Turn off the gas, slide a lid or damp fire blanket over it. Do not carry it.

say: Never fill a pot more than about one third with oil. Keep the handle turned in, lower food gently, keep children away, and never leave hot oil, even for a phone call.

cards.d: Most frying works at about 160 to 180 C. Fry small batches, golden not dark brown.
Oil no more than one third of the pot. Handle turned in. Never leave hot oil alone.
Never use water. Turn off the gas, slide a lid or damp fire blanket over it. Do not carry it.

say: If oil catches fire, never pour water on it. It throws flaming oil across the room. Turn off the gas if you can reach it safely, slide a metal lid or a damp fire blanket over the pot, and leave it covered until cool.

say: To remember. Start stock in cold water, simmer gently and do not salt it. Give tough cuts long, gentle, moist heat.
Check chicken and fish reach at least 70 C. Use charcoal outdoors only. And never put water on an oil fire.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Stock: cold water start, gentle simmer, no salt
Tough cuts: long, gentle, moist heat
Chicken and fish: at least 70 C inside
Charcoal outdoors only
Oil fire: cover it, never water
